  Sources: memory/active_projects.md

args.title: How an LLM server shares one GPU: scheduling, paged KV cache, and prefix caching
args.markdown:
Your TTFT tripled at 3pm and your prompt did not change. Your code sent the same bytes, at the same rate, with the same key. The provider returned the same answer, three times slower. Nothing on your side explains it. The explanation is not on your side. It sits in the requests that arrived at the same second as yours.

A single request has a simple model: time to first token (TTFT), time per output token after the first (TPOT), and the bill. That model is correct but not complete. A real inference server never runs one request. It runs a loop over a batch. Your request shares a GPU with requests from other people. This post opens that loop and answers two questions:

- Why did my TTFT triple at 3pm when my prompt did not change?
- Why does the same prompt cost 4x less on the second call, and how do I make that happen every time?

## The scheduler loop: your latency depends on other requests

vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and hosted providers all run the same loop. The names differ. The steps are the same. Three terms:

- **Prefill** is the pass that reads your whole prompt. It produces the first token.
- **Decode** is each later pass. Each decode pass produces one more token.
- A **forward pass** is one run of the model over a set of tokens.

One scheduler iteration:

1. Look at the waiting queue and the running set.
2. Pick work that fits a token budget and a memory budget.
3. Run one forward pass over all of it together.
4. Every decoding request gets exactly one new token.
5. Finished requests leave; freed memory returns to the pool.
6. Go to step 1.

Step 4 surprises most people. One iteration produces one token per request. The batch size does not change this. A batch of 40 requests produces 40 tokens, and that takes about the time one request takes for 1 token.

The reason is what a decode step does. It reads all the model weights from GPU memory once. Then it does a small amount of arithmetic per sequence. The memory read takes most of the time. One more sequence adds only a little arithmetic. A simple cost model makes this concrete: with a base decode cost of 18.0ms for a batch of 1 and 0.12ms per additional sequence, a batch of 16 decoding requests costs 18.0 + 0.12 x 16 = 19.92ms per iteration. A batch of 1 costs 18.12ms. Sixteen times the tokens cost 10% more time.

### Static batching was the old way

The server collected N requests and ran them together. It admitted no new request until the last one in the batch finished. A finished request kept holding its slot, and its GPU memory, until the slowest request in the batch was done. The idle spans are the whole problem: a slot is GPU memory plus a place in the batch, and static batching releases neither when its request finishes.

### Continuous batching is the current way

The scheduler admits new work on every iteration. A finished request leaves at once. A waiting request takes its slot on the next step. This method is called iteration-level scheduling. The Orca paper introduced it in 2022 (OSDI 2022, usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu). The paper's headline, with conditions: FasterTransformer served 0.185 requests per second at a median normalised latency of 190ms, and Orca served 6.81, a 36.9x speedup on GPT-3 175B in fp16 on 16 A100 40GB GPUs, with inputs of 32 to 512 tokens and outputs of 1 to 128.

A toy simulator with the cost model above, at 40 requests and 6 arrivals per second, shows the shape of the real effect:

| policy | mean TTFT | p99 TTFT | mean TPOT | worst gap | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| static | 5,357ms | 9,215ms | 19.4ms | 20ms | 2.3 rq/s |
| continuous | 867ms | 2,649ms | 25.4ms | 764ms | 3.6 rq/s |

Three effects:

- Mean TTFT fell from 5,357ms to 867ms, about 6.2x better.
- Throughput rose from 2.3 to 3.6 requests per second, 57% more.
- Mean TPOT rose from 19.4ms to 25.4ms. A fuller batch decodes each token a little slower.

The third effect is not a bug. You traded a slower token for a 6x better TTFT. Anyscale measured the same progression on real hardware (anyscale.com/blog/continuous-batching-llm-inference, OPT-13B on one A100 40GB, 1,000 requests, 512 input tokens): up to 23x throughput with continuous batching plus paged memory, up to 8x from continuous batching alone, against simple static batching as the baseline. Always quote the 23x with that baseline.

### The arrival pattern is what you feel

Run the same workload at 12 arrivals per second instead of 6. Continuous batching mean TTFT rises from 867ms to 1,674ms. Static rises from 5,357ms to 6,551ms. The prompts did not change. Only the arrival rate changed. This is the answer to "why did my TTFT triple at 3pm": your request shares a longer queue.

What you control on a hosted API: prompt length (a long prefill uses the token budget and delays every decoding request), output length (a long generation holds a slot and its KV memory), arrival pattern (50 requests at once wait; 50 spread out do not), and prefix reuse (a cached prefix skips prefill).

**The trap:** you will try to fix a TTFT spike with retries. A retry adds one more request to the same queue. Under load, the queue gets longer and the spike gets worse.

The server side has the matching fix: admission control. vLLM 0.29.0 added two flags, `--max-num-queued-reqs` and `--max-num-queued-tokens`. When the queue limit is hit, a new request is rejected with HTTP 503 instead of queueing forever. If you self-host, serving a 503 and letting the client back off beats a silent queue. (Verified in vllm/config/scheduler.py at tag v0.29.0.)

The sentence to remember: one scheduler iteration gives every running request one token. Throughput comes from batch size. Latency comes from what else is in the batch.

## The paged KV cache: why the server fits 18x more requests

The KV cache holds the key and value vectors of every token the model has seen. The model reads them on every decode step, so they must stay in GPU memory. How many requests fit at once, the concurrency, decides how long requests wait in queue.

Start with the simple allocator, because it shows the problem. The server admits a request and does not know how long the answer will be. So it reserves memory for the worst case: max_model_len, the longest sequence the server accepts. For llama-3-8b, the KV cache costs 2 (K and V) x 8 KV heads x 128 head dim x 2 bytes (fp16) x 32 layers = 131,072 bytes per token, so a 32,768-token reservation holds 4.00 GB. A 56 GB KV pool then admits 14 concurrent requests, and 52.9 GB sits idle.

PagedAttention fixes this with an idea from operating system virtual memory. The KV cache of one sequence does not need one continuous region. The server splits the cache into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens), allocates a block only when the sequence needs it, and keeps a block table for each sequence that maps logical positions to physical blocks. Blocks need not be adjacent, and nothing is reserved for the future.

Same hardware, llama-3-8b on one 80GB GPU, requests holding about 1,800 tokens:

| | contiguous | paged |
|---|---|---|
| reserved per request | 32,768 tok | 1,808 tok |
| bytes per request | 4.00 GB | 0.22 GB |
| concurrent requests | 14 | 253 |
| memory actually used | 3.1 GB | 55.6 GB |
| memory wasted | 52.9 GB | 0.2 GB |

Paging admits 18.1x more concurrent requests. The model and GPU did not change. The paper measured the underlying waste in real systems: only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV cache memory held real token state; reserved slots and fragmentation used the rest (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023, arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180). The authors state that paging cut that waste to about 4%; no written measurement method was found, so treat the exact figure as their claim.

Three facts to remember:

- **Block size sets the remaining waste.** A request holding 1,800 tokens needs 113 blocks of 16 tokens, which is 1,808 slots. The 8 unused slots are internal fragmentation, the only waste paging leaves.
- **Identical blocks can be shared.** Two requests with the same first 1,200 tokens can point at the same physical blocks. The prefix is stored once.
- **When blocks run out, the server does not error. It preempts.** It frees a running sequence's blocks and puts the request back in the queue. On resume it must redo the prefill it threw away. The user sees the answer stop mid-stream, then continue. TTFT and total latency do not show this. Only an inter-token gap metric shows it.

The paper's section 4.5 names the rules: scheduling is first-come-first-served, the latest-arrived requests are preempted first, all of a sequence's blocks are freed together, and recovery is either swapping KV blocks to CPU RAM or recomputing them. vLLM's recompute path is PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE.

That preemption path has a production failure worth knowing: preemption-recompute thrash. max_num_seqs sets how many sequences run; the KV pool size sets how many fit. If the first limit is looser than the second, the scheduler over-admits, preempts running sequences, they re-prefill, and they recreate the pressure that evicted them. Throughput collapses while GPU utilisation stays high, so the dashboard looks healthy. No error is ever raised. The documented fix is to lower `--max-num-seqs`, not to raise the memory pool. To confirm it, halve concurrency and watch throughput go up. This comes from a vendor failure encyclopedia (denpex.com/failures/vllm-preemption-recompute-thrash) whose exact log-line and counter names I could not verify against the source tree; the mechanism is consistent with the vLLM scheduler source, and the remedy detail is gated behind a signup, so verify the signatures on your own server.

Sharing changes the capacity number a lot. If every request shares the same first 1,200 tokens: the 56 GB pool holds 28,672 blocks of 16 tokens at 128 KB per token. The shared prefix is 1,200 / 16 = 75 blocks, stored once. Each request needs ceil(600 / 16) = 38 private blocks. So (28,672 - 75) / 38 = 752 concurrent requests, up from 253. Concurrency is arithmetic you can do before you buy hardware.

One capacity setting is widely misunderstood. `gpu_memory_utilization` looks like a safety setting. It works as a capacity setting. vLLM 0.29.0 defaults it to 0.92 (verified in vllm/config/cache.py; any tutorial quoting 0.90 as current is stale). Lowering it to 0.70 on an 80GB GPU removes 17.6 GB from the KV pool. For llama-3-8b at 1,808 tokens per request, concurrency falls from 260 to 181 requests: 30% of your capacity, from a config line.

The sentence to remember: paging reserves only the memory a request needs now, not the most it could need. That change makes high concurrency possible.

## Prefix caching inside the server: the radix tree and the eviction that ends it

Identical blocks can be shared, but the server needs a fast way to find them. It keeps a tree keyed by the token sequence. SGLang calls its version RadixAttention. vLLM calls it automatic prefix caching. The structure is the same.

Picture three requests that share a 1,200-token system prompt. The prompt's 75 blocks hang off the root, stored once. Each user's private history hangs below. A new request walks down from the root, reuses every node it matches, and stops at the first block that differs. Everything below that is a miss.

The matching rule has three parts, and teams lose money on each:

1. **Matching starts at token 0 and moves forward.** There is no match that starts in the middle. A change at position 10 ends the match for positions 10 to the end. The block hash includes the parent block's hash, so an identical block after a difference has a different key. A match cannot restart.
2. **Matching happens in whole blocks.** A 1,210-token prefix with 16-token blocks shares only 75 full blocks, 1,200 tokens. The last 10 tokens sit in a partial block and are not cached. vLLM's design doc says this in its own words: "we only cache full blocks".
3. **Entries leave the cache.** The tree has a fixed size and evicts least recently used blocks first. Hosted providers also expire entries after a time limit, commonly a few minutes without use.

### The layout cost, measured

A simulation of an agent loop with two layouts holding the same information, 30 requests, priced at gpt-4.1-mini rates ($0.40 per million input tokens, cached tokens at 0.25x):

| layout | input toks | cached toks | hit rate | cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| volatile-first | 148,560 | 0 | 0.0% | $0.0594 |
| stable-first | 148,560 | 136,656 | 92.0% | $0.0184 |

Stable-first costs 3.22x less. The only change was the order of the parts. The wrong version puts a timestamp at the top of the system message, so byte ~40 changes on every call and every later block misses. It fails without a sign: no error, no warning, a bill 3x higher, and nothing in your logs says why.

Put what never changes first. Put what changes on every call last.

### Eviction: your hit rate depends on other tenants

A correct layout still loses its hits when the cache fills. In the same simulation, a workload that hits 93.5% with no size limit falls to 68.8% when the cache holds only 500 blocks (5,615 evictions), and to 0.0% at 200 blocks. Your prompt did not change. Other conversations filled the cache.

Real deployments report a similar range. The SGLang paper measured hit rates on Chatbot Arena traffic of 52.4% for LLaVA-Next-34B and 74.1% for Vicuna-33B, with a 50% to 99% range across benchmarks (arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104). A hit rate near 100% comes from a synthetic test. Production traffic rarely shows it. So never build a cost model that assumes a hit. Model both prices and alert on the hit rate.

### A production story in Go

One engineer ran a coding agent through a Bifrost gateway and vLLM 0.28.0 (doug.sh/posts/vllm-kv-cache-agents, one deployment, one model). His cached share rose from 55% to 95%. Average wait for the first word fell from 26 to 28 seconds to 7.3 seconds; the worst wait fell from 514 seconds to 54 seconds.

The biggest cache-breaker was not his prompt design. The mcp-go library decodes tool schemas into Go maps. Go map iteration order is randomised. The gateway re-serialised the maps in whatever order they came out, so the tool schema bytes shuffled on every process start. The schemas sit at the top of the prompt, and one shuffle invalidated everything after them. A single workaround, `tojson(sort_keys=True)`, moved the cached share from 78% to 95%. Fixes landed upstream as bifrost#7170 and mcp-go#984. If you build agents in Go, sort your keys before you serialise anything that goes into a prompt.

Two more lessons from the same incident. Block granularity is model-dependent: his hybrid linear-attention model cached in 2,048-token blocks, not 16, and CPU KV offloading was nearly useless there (about 40 GB copied out and about 250 MB restored in an hour). And his measurement recipe: hit rate is cached tokens divided by total prompt tokens, not a count. You find a miss cause by diffing two consecutive tokenised prompts to the first differing token, on an idle server, before you blame eviction.

## What I could not verify

The Orca paper's 36.9x headline is confirmed from its abstract and introduction, but its evaluation section was not readable, so the 0.185 req/s and 190ms baseline conditions are unverified. The "under 4% waste" figure for paging is the vLLM authors' own claim; no written measurement method exists. The Denpex log-line and Prometheus counter names were not checked against source. And the live-concurrency experiment (eight parallel TTFT measurements against a hosted API) was never run; its cost was estimated at about $0.05.

## Takeaways

- One scheduler iteration gives every running request one token. Your TTFT is a function of other people's traffic. Never answer a TTFT spike with retries; they lengthen the queue. If you self-host, reject with 503 and let clients back off.
- Concurrency is memory arithmetic. Paging reserves what a request needs now, not the worst case. `gpu_memory_utilization` is a capacity dial: moving it from 0.92 to 0.70 costs about 30% of concurrent requests.
- The prefix cache matches whole blocks from token 0 forward, with hash chains that cannot restart after a miss, under LRU eviction. Prompt order is a pricing decision, a cache hit is never guaranteed, and in Go, unsorted map serialisation at the top of a prompt silently costs you 3x.

I am not writing today's article. Here is why, and what the material actually contains.

## What the digest holds

The whole of hunter's digest (`quarantine/eval-thin-digest.md`) is this:

- One blog post (a placeholder URL, `https://example.com/post`) claiming chunked prefill "helps latency".
- No numbers. No hardware. No serving-stack version. No workload description.
- "Nothing else was found."

A note at the top of my own rules covers exactly this: a lesson is written only from what the note supports, and a fact the note does not support stays off the page.

## What the assignment needs versus what exists

The planned article was a *measured* comparison of chunked prefill budgets on one real server, in the "measures" relationship to Phase 2A (scheduling and memory). The word "measured" is the load-bearing one. It needs, at minimum:

- A prefill-chunk size swept across at least two or three budgets (tokens per step).
- For each: TTFT, ITL or end-to-end latency, on named hardware, with a named serving framework and version.
- A workload: prompt lengths, output lengths, concurrency.

The digest has none of these. It has one unattributed qualitative claim. If I wrote the article anyway, every table, every number and every "on an A100 with vLLM 0.6" would be invented. That is the one thing I must not do, and it is worse than no article: an invented measurement is what Phase 2A exists to teach him to distrust.

## What I am doing instead

Nothing is written to the repo. Nothing is filed as taught, so tomorrow's scan does not believe this topic is covered.

Two notes for you:

1. **Reading ledger.** The source post should stay marked un-taught (or be skipped explicitly), so this slot re-opens when real material lands.
2. **What would unblock it.** A single source with an actual chunked-prefill measurement is enough. Good candidates for hunter's next sweep: the vLLM chunked-prefill RFC or release benchmarks, the Sarathi-Serve paper (it is the origin of the technique and ships TTFT/throughput curves on A100s), or the DistServe paper for prefill/decode interference numbers. Any one of these supports the "measures" article properly.

A quiet article day, honestly reported, costs you two minutes. A fabricated benchmark table would cost you the habit of trusting these pages.

Add as a standing rule, via sage: "When a digest is thinner than the article's claim requires, tutor stops and reports the gap instead of writing; the thin-material case is a skip, not a prompt to pad."
